claim: NusA and NusG are transcription factors that stimulate RNA polymerase pausing in Bacillus subtilis.
source: NusA and NusG are transcription factors that stimulate RNA polymerase pausing in Bacillus subtilis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about these proteins.

claim: NusA was known to function as an intrinsic termination factor in B. subtilis prior to this study.
source: While NusA was known to function as an intrinsic termination factor in B. subtilis, the role of NusG in this process was unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as prior knowledge, with citation support provided in the introduction.

claim: The role of NusG in intrinsic termination in B. subtilis was unknown prior to this study.
source: While NusA was known to function as an intrinsic termination factor in B. subtilis, the role of NusG in this process was unknown.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as the knowledge gap addressed by this study.

claim: Term-seq was conducted in wild type, NusA depletion, ΔnusG, and NusA depletion ΔnusG strains.
source: To examine the individual and combinatorial roles that NusA and NusG play in intrinsic termination, Term-seq was conducted in wild type, NusA depletion, ΔnusG, and NusA depletion ΔnusG strains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and described in detail in the methods section.

claim: NusG functions as an intrinsic termination factor.
source: We determined that NusG functions as an intrinsic termination factor that works alone and cooperatively with NusA to facilitate termination at 88% of the 1400 identified intrinsic terminators.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by Term-seq data throughout the manuscript.

claim: NusG works cooperatively with NusA to facilitate termination at 88% of the 1400 identified intrinsic terminators.
source: We determined that NusG functions as an intrinsic termination factor that works alone and cooperatively with NusA to facilitate termination at 88% of the 1400 identified intrinsic terminators.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative Term-seq data.

claim: 1400 intrinsic terminators were identified in this study.
source: We determined that NusG functions as an intrinsic termination factor that works alone and cooperatively with NusA to facilitate termination at 88% of the 1400 identified intrinsic terminators.
evidence: This number is stated in the abstract and detailed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: NusG stimulates a sequence-specific pause that assists in the completion of suboptimal terminator hairpins.
source: Our results indicate that NusG stimulates a sequence-specific pause that assists in the completion of suboptimal terminator hairpins with weak terminal A-U and G-U base pairs at the bottom of the stem.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro transcription experiments.

claim: NusG-dependent terminators have weak terminal A-U and G-U base pairs at the bottom of the stem.
source: Our results indicate that NusG stimulates a sequence-specific pause that assists in the completion of suboptimal terminator hairpins with weak terminal A-U and G-U base pairs at the bottom of the stem.
evidence: This is a structural characteristic identified through analysis of terminator sequences and supported by Figure 4 and related data.

claim: Loss of NusA and NusG leads to global misregulation of gene expression.
source: Loss of NusA and NusG leads to global misregulation of gene expression and loss of NusG results in flagella and swimming motility defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of NusG results in flagella and swimming motility defects.
source: Loss of NusA and NusG leads to global misregulation of gene expression and loss of NusG results in flagella and swimming motility defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by swimming motility assays and fluorescence microscopy in Figure 7.

claim: Rho-dependent termination requires the activity of Rho, a hexameric ATP-dependent RNA translocase.
source: One mechanism is Rho-dependent termination, which requires the activity of Rho, a hexameric ATP-dependent RNA translocase (Roberts, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Roberts, 2019.

claim: Intrinsic termination is generally assumed to not require the activity of additional protein factors.
source: The other mechanism is intrinsic termination, which is generally assumed to not require the activity of additional protein factors and as such is also frequently referred to as factor-independent termination (Roberts, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a general assumption in the field, cited from Roberts, 2019.

claim: An intrinsic terminator is composed of a GC-rich hairpin followed immediately by a U-rich tract.
source: An intrinsic terminator is composed of a GC-rich hairpin followed immediately by a U-rich tract, both of which define the point of termination (POT) (Roberts, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about intrinsic terminator structure, cited from Roberts, 2019.

claim: NusA is a conserved bacterial transcription elongation factor that is essential for cellular viability in both Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli.
source: NusA is a conserved bacterial transcription elongation factor that is essential for cellular viability in both Bacillus subtilis and Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: NusA binds to the flap-tip domain of the β subunit of RNAP via its N-terminal domain (NTD).
source: This protein factor binds to the flap-tip domain of the β subunit of RNAP via its N-terminal domain (NTD) (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 2018.

claim: NusA can directly interact with RNA using its S1, KH1, and KH2 domains.
source: Once bound, NusA can directly interact with RNA using its S1, KH1, and KH2 domains (Guo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from Guo et al., 2018.

claim: NusG is the only universally conserved transcription factor.
source: NusG, or SPT5 in archaeal and eukaryotic organisms, is the only universally conserved transcription factor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Bacterial NusG has two domains: the N-terminal NGN domain and the KOW domain.
source: Bacterial NusG has two domains: the N-terminal NGN domain, which binds to the clamp helices of the β' subunit of RNAP, and the KOW domain, which is connected to the NGN domain via a flexible linker and is free to interact with various regulatory partners (Liu and Steitz, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Liu and Steitz, 2017.

claim: The NGN domain of NusG binds to the clamp helices of the β' subunit of RNAP.
source: Bacterial NusG has two domains: the N-terminal NGN domain, which binds to the clamp helices of the β' subunit of RNAP, and the KOW domain, which is connected to the NGN domain via a flexible linker and is free to interact with various regulatory partners (Liu and Steitz, 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Liu and Steitz, 2017.

claim: B. subtilis NusG is a sequence-specific pausing factor due to the ability of its NGN domain to make direct contacts with the non-template DNA (ntDNA) strand within the transcription bubble.
source: In contrast, B. subtilis NusG is a sequence-specific pausing factor due to the ability of its NGN domain to make direct contacts with the non-template DNA (ntDNA) strand within the transcription bubble (Yakhnin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Yakhnin et al., 2016.

claim: B. subtilis NusG elicits a pause when the NGN domain encounters a stretch of T residues at critically conserved positions.
source: This interaction results in a pause when the NGN domain encounters a stretch of T residues at critically conserved positions, as observed in 1600 NusG-dependent pause sites genome-wide (Yakhnin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Yakhnin et al., 2020.

claim: 1600 NusG-dependent pause sites were identified genome-wide in B. subtilis.
source: This interaction results in a pause when the NGN domain encounters a stretch of T residues at critically conserved positions, as observed in 1600 NusG-dependent pause sites genome-wide (Yakhnin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from Yakhnin et al., 2020.

claim: NusA can stimulate intrinsic termination of E. coli and B. subtilis RNAP in vitro.
source: While intrinsic termination does not require additional auxiliary protein factors, it has been known for many years that NusA can stimulate intrinsic termination of E. coli and B. subtilis RNAP in vitro (Greenblatt et al., 1981; Schmidt and Chamberlin, 1987; Bermúdez-Cruz et al., 1999; Yakhnin and Babitzke, 2002).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Greenblatt et al., 1981; Schmidt and Chamberlin, 1987; Bermúdez-Cruz et al., 1999; Yakhnin and Babitzke, 2002.

claim: Mycobacterial NusG can stimulate intrinsic termination in vitro.
source: The ability of mycobacterial NusG to stimulate intrinsic termination in vitro has also been reported (Czyz et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Czyz et al., 2014.

claim: NusA stimulates intrinsic termination in vivo on a global level in B. subtilis, with 232 intrinsic terminators classified as NusA-dependent.
source: More recently it was determined that NusA stimulates intrinsic termination in vivo on a global level in B. subtilis, with 232 intrinsic terminators classified as NusA-dependent (Mondal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Mondal et al., 2016.

claim: Only 12% of all identified intrinsic terminators continue to terminate efficiently in the absence of both NusA and NusG.
source: Our results suggest a model in which NusG-dependent pausing plays a vital role in NusG-dependent termination, and that the absence of NusG results in the misregulation of global gene expression and altered cellular physiology and behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1B where 12% of terminators are classified as independent in the double mutant.

claim: Growth of the nusAdep strain in the absence of IPTG results in depletion of NusA to less than 2% of WT levels within four cell generations.
source: Thus, growth in the presence of IPTG results in wild-type (WT) levels of NusA, whereas growth in the absence of IPTG results in depletion of NusA to less than 2% of WT levels within four cell generations as shown via Western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by Western blot in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4657 3' ends were identified in the WT strain.
source: Using this system, we identified 4657 3' ends in the WT strain (Supplementary file 1), 1400 of which were categorized as intrinsic terminators (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: NusG stimulated intrinsic termination to a similar extent as NusA, with an ~22% drop in median %T in the nusAdep and ΔnusG strains when compared to the WT strain.
source: NusG stimulated intrinsic termination to a similar extent as NusA, with an ~ 22% drop in median %T in the nusAdep and ΔnusG strains when compared to the WT strain.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss of both NusA and NusG in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain resulted in a drastic termination defect, with the median %T falling 55%.
source: Loss of both NusA and NusG in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain resulted in a drastic termination defect, with the median %T falling 55%.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 65% of all intrinsic terminators are present in the Req A and G or in the Req A or G subpopulations.
source: Intriguingly, 65% of all intrinsic terminators depicted in Figure 1B are present in the Req A and G or in the Req A or G subpopulations, clearly illustrating a large functional overlap between NusA and NusG on intrinsic termination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be calculated from the Venn diagram in Figure 1B.

claim: Terminators that require NusG in any fashion have weaker predicted hairpins than SI terminators.
source: It was found that terminators that require NusG in any fashion have weaker predicted hairpins than SI terminators, akin to Req A terminators, while terminators that require both NusA and NusG have the weakest hairpins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Terminators that require both NusA and NusG have the weakest hairpins.
source: It was found that terminators that require NusG in any fashion have weaker predicted hairpins than SI terminators, akin to Req A terminators, while terminators that require both NusA and NusG have the weakest hairpins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Terminators that require NusG in any fashion exhibit a stronger enrichment of U residues downstream of the predicted hairpin than Req A terminators.
source: In addition, terminators that require NusG in any fashion exhibit a stronger enrichment of U residues downstream of the predicted hairpin than Req A terminators (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: SI terminators have longer hairpin stems than all subpopulations except Req A or G terminators, with a median of 10 nt.
source: Analyzing the distribution of predicted terminator hairpin stem lengths from each subpopulation with Fisher-Pitman permutation testing shows that SI terminators have longer hairpin stems than all subpopulations except Req A or G terminators, with a median of 10 nt (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: NusG recapitulated the stimulatory effect on termination of the yetJ and ktrD terminators, as well as the cooperative effect between NusA and NusG observed in vivo.
source: NusG recapitulated the stimulatory effect on termination of the yetJ and ktrD terminators, as well as the cooperative effect between NusA and NusG that we observed in vivo (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The NGN domain of NusG is sufficient to recapitulate the stimulatory effect on termination.
source: Moreover, the highly similar termination patterns observed when using either full-length NusG or the NGN domain (± NusA) demonstrate that this phenomenon can be fully attributed to the NGN domain of NusG (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The mutant NGN domain (Y77H/N81S/T82V) lacks either a stimulatory effect on termination or a cooperative effect on termination with NusA.
source: The lack of either a stimulatory effect on termination or a cooperative effect on termination with NusA by the mutant NGN domain indicates that the effect of NusG on termination can be explained through its role as a pausing factor (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The effect of NusG on termination can be explained through its role as a pausing factor.
source: The lack of either a stimulatory effect on termination or a cooperative effect on termination with NusA by the mutant NGN domain indicates that the effect of NusG on termination can be explained through its role as a pausing factor (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion stated in the results and supported by the mutant NGN domain experiments in Figure 2C and F.

claim: NusG elicits three consecutive NusG-dependent transcription products at the ktrD terminator that are 9, 10, and 11 nt downstream from the predicted terminator hairpin.
source: Results from this assay revealed three consecutive NusG-dependent transcription products that were 9, 10, and 11 nt downstream from the predicted terminator hairpin.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The product 9 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent termination site (POT1).
source: Comparing the RNA species in the time course lanes with the 30 min termination lane shows that the product 9 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent termination site (POT1), the product 10 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site and a NusG-dependent termination site (Pause1/POT2), and the product 11 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site (Pause2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The product 10 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site and a NusG-dependent termination site (Pause1/POT2).
source: Comparing the RNA species in the time course lanes with the 30 min termination lane shows that the product 9 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent termination site (POT1), the product 10 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site and a NusG-dependent termination site (Pause1/POT2), and the product 11 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site (Pause2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The product 11 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site (Pause2).
source: Comparing the RNA species in the time course lanes with the 30 min termination lane shows that the product 9 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent termination site (POT1), the product 10 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site and a NusG-dependent termination site (Pause1/POT2), and the product 11 nt from the predicted hairpin is a NusG-dependent pause site (Pause2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The hairpin to 3' end distance for intrinsic terminators is 7–9 nt.
source: The hairpin to 3' end distance for intrinsic terminators is 7–9 nt, whereas this distance is 11–12 nt for pause sites (Mondal et al., 2016; Yakhnin et al., 2020; Ray-Soni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Mondal et al., 2016; Yakhnin et al., 2020; Ray-Soni et al., 2016.

claim: The hairpin to 3' end distance for pause sites is 11–12 nt.
source: The hairpin to 3' end distance for intrinsic terminators is 7–9 nt, whereas this distance is 11–12 nt for pause sites (Mondal et al., 2016; Yakhnin et al., 2020; Ray-Soni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Mondal et al., 2016; Yakhnin et al., 2020; Ray-Soni et al., 2016.

claim: The NusG-dependent pause motif is sufficient to elicit a pause and the position of this pause is set by the motif.
source: These results indicate that the NusG-dependent pause motif upstream of the 3' end is sufficient to elicit a pause and that the position of this pause is set by the motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the mutant ktrD terminator experiments.

claim: The duration of the pauses on the mutant ktrD template was shorter than the pauses on the WT template.
source: Calculating the half-life of both pauses on each template revealed that the duration of the pauses on the mutant template was shorter than the pauses on the WT template, implying that a NusG-dependent pause can be stabilized to different degrees by hairpins of different lengths and strengths.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: A NusG-dependent pause can be stabilized to different degrees by hairpins of different lengths and strengths.
source: Calculating the half-life of both pauses on each template revealed that the duration of the pauses on the mutant template was shorter than the pauses on the WT template, implying that a NusG-dependent pause can be stabilized to different degrees by hairpins of different lengths and strengths.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on pause half-life measurements.

claim: Termination occurring 7–9 nt downstream of the hairpin is a biophysical constraint set by the length of the RNA-DNA hybrid when RNAP is in the post-translocated state.
source: Termination occurring 7–9 nt downstream of the hairpin is a biophysical constraint set by the length of the RNA-DNA hybrid when RNAP is in the post-translocated state (Ray-Soni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Ray-Soni et al., 2016.

claim: NusG effectively stimulated termination in vitro at a POT that utilized hairpins with two to four consecutive A-U base pairs at the bottom of the hairpin stem.
source: Notably, in all cases NusG effectively stimulated termination in vitro at a POT that utilized hairpins with two to four consecutive A-U base pairs at the bottom of the hairpin stem.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NusG stimulated the fur terminator in vitro to terminate at a position 9 nt downstream of a hairpin that utilized a G-U base pair at the bottom of the hairpin stem.
source: Interestingly, we also found that NusG stimulated the fur terminator in vitro to terminate at a position 9 nt downstream of a hairpin that utilized a G-U base pair at the bottom of the hairpin stem (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Termination in vitro occurred at a position 1–3 nt further downstream than the 3' end identified in vivo by Term-seq on all templates tested.
source: We found that termination in vitro occurred at a position 1–3 nt further downstream than the 3' end identified in vivo by Term-seq on all templates tested (Figures 3B, 4B and E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in multiple figures.

claim: 485 peaks of nascent RNET-seq 3' ends were identified located 0–4 nt downstream of the 3' end of an intrinsic terminator identified by Term-seq.
source: Using our published RNET-seq data from WT B. subtilis (Yakhnin et al., 2020), we identified 485 peaks of nascent RNET-seq 3' ends located 0–4 nt downstream of the 3' end of an intrinsic terminator identified by Term-seq (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and documented in Supplementary file 4.

claim: For 82% of the 485 RNET-seq 3' ends at intrinsic terminators, the RNET-seq 3' end was 1–4 nt downstream of the Term-seq 3' end.
source: Notably, for 82% of these 3' ends, the RNET-seq 3' end was 1–4 nt downstream of the Term-seq 3' end (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: NusG-dependent terminators were more likely to contain ≥1 consecutive terminal A-U/G-U base pairs than SI of NusG terminators.
source: For these revised terminators, the SI of NusG terminators were directly compared to the NusG-dependent terminators via a Fisher's exact test, which revealed that NusG-dependent terminators were more likely to contain ≥1 consecutive terminal A-U/G-U base pairs than SI of NusG terminators (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: NusG-dependent terminators exhibited a modest tendency to have distal U-rich tract interruptions compared to SI of NusG terminators.
source: Generating sequence logos for the SI of NusG and NusG-dependent terminators from this updated pool and comparing these logos using DiffLogo (Nettling et al., 2015) showed that NusG-dependent terminators exhibited a modest tendency to have distal U-rich tract interruptions compared to SI of NusG terminators (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 106 transcripts increased in expression and 37 transcripts decreased in expression in the ΔnusG strain.
source: This approach revealed that NusG is involved in regulating gene expression on a global scale, with 106 transcripts increasing in expression and 37 transcripts decreasing in expression in the ΔnusG strain (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 322 transcripts increased in expression and 94 transcripts decreased in expression in the nusAdep strain.
source: NusA had a larger effect on gene expression with 322 transcripts increasing in expression and 94 transcripts decreasing in expression in the nusAdep strain (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 28% of all transcripts expressed in the WT strain were misregulated in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain.
source: The cooperative relationship between those two proteins on intrinsic termination extended to gene expression, with 28% of all transcripts expressed in the WT strain being misregulated in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Loss of NusG resulted in a median threefold decrease in expression of genes within the motility regulon.
source: Through this analysis, it was found that loss of NusG resulted in a median threefold decrease in expression of genes within the motility regulon, while loss of both NusA and NusG resulted in a median eightfold decrease in expression of these genes (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Loss of both NusA and NusG resulted in a median eightfold decrease in expression of genes within the motility regulon.
source: Through this analysis, it was found that loss of NusG resulted in a median threefold decrease in expression of genes within the motility regulon, while loss of both NusA and NusG resulted in a median eightfold decrease in expression of these genes (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The fla/che operon is composed of 32 genes involved in flagella biosynthesis and motility.
source: The 27 kb fla/che operon is composed of 32 genes involved in flagella biosynthesis and motility (Cozy and Kearns, 2010; Márquez-Magaña and Chamberlin, 1994; Albertini et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Cozy and Kearns, 2010; Márquez-Magaña and Chamberlin, 1994; Albertini et al., 1991.

claim: Expression of flgC decreased 1.7-fold in the ΔnusG strain.
source: We found that for the majority of matched 3' ends, the distance between the previously identified and currently identified 3' ends was 0–1 nt. For all newly identified 3' ends, the %T was calculated based on the position of the newly identified 3' end.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Expression of sigD decreased threefold in the ΔnusG strain.
source: To assess the expression trends of the fla/che operon, expression of the second gene of the cluster (flgC) and sigD was calculated, showing a 1.7-fold and threefold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the ΔnusG strain, respectively, and a 2.1-fold and 10-fold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain, respectively (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Expression of flgC decreased 2.1-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain.
source: To assess the expression trends of the fla/che operon, expression of the second gene of the cluster (flgC) and sigD was calculated, showing a 1.7-fold and threefold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the ΔnusG strain, respectively, and a 2.1-fold and 10-fold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain, respectively (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Expression of sigD decreased 10-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain.
source: To assess the expression trends of the fla/che operon, expression of the second gene of the cluster (flgC) and sigD was calculated, showing a 1.7-fold and threefold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the ΔnusG strain, respectively, and a 2.1-fold and 10-fold decrease in the expression of flgC and sigD in the in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain, respectively (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: The ratio of flgC to sigD expression increased from 1.3-fold in the WT strain to 2.1-fold in the ΔnusG strain and 6.2-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain.
source: As such, the ratio of flgC to sigD expression increased from 1.3-fold in the WT strain to 2.1-fold in the ΔnusG strain and 6.2-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Expression of hag mRNA was reduced 4-fold in the ΔnusG strain and by 75-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain.
source: Consistent with a cascading reduction in expression of the σD regulon due to the reduction of sigD expression, expression of hag mRNA was reduced 4-fold in the ΔnusG strain and by 75-fold in the nusAdep ΔnusG strain (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Loss of NusG results in both a decrease in the frequency of cells that produced flagella and a reduced number of flagella per cell.
source: Through this experiment, we observed both a decrease in the frequency of cells that produced flagella and a reduced number of flagella per cell.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: B. subtilis NusA and NusG likely work together without physical interaction to cooperatively stimulate termination in vivo.
source: While the AR2 domain of NusA and the NGN domain of NusG were found to physically interact in E. coli during elongation, this interaction is unlikely to be relevant to the regulation of elongation in B. subtilis due to the absence of the AR2 domain in B. subtilis NusA (Strauß et al., 2016). Thus, B. subtilis NusA and NusG likely work together without physical interaction to cooperatively stimulate termination in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the absence of the AR2 domain in B. subtilis NusA.

claim: Intrinsic (factor-independent) termination is primarily a factor-mediated process in B. subtilis.
source: Thus, our results establish that intrinsic (factor-independent) termination is primarily a factor-mediated process in B. subtilis.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the discussion based on the finding that only 12% of terminators are independent of both NusA and NusG.

claim: NusA is the more potent termination factor in vitro compared to NusG.
source: In vitro experimentation was conducted on six terminators that were found to be stimulated by NusG in vivo, and it was generally found that NusA is the more potent termination factor in vitro (Figure 2, Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in multiple figures.

claim: NusG shifts RNAP to the post-translocation register in both E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: This finding can be explained by the fact that NusG shifts RNAP to the post-translocation register in both E. coli and B. subtilis (Sevostyanova and Artsimovitch, 2010; Yakhnin et al., 2020), and may thus function as a processivity factor in B. subtilis until encountering the consensus pause motif at these terminators.
evidence: This is cited from Sevostyanova and Artsimovitch, 2010; Yakhnin et al., 2020.

claim: The discrepancy between the in vivo released POT(s) and in vivo nascent POT(s) can likely be attributed to exoribonuclease trimming of the terminated transcripts in vivo.
source: The discrepancy between the in vivo released POT(s) and in vivo nascent POT(s) can likely be attributed to exoribonuclease trimming of the terminated transcripts in vivo, which has shown to occur via YhaM-mediated degradation in the related firmicute Streptococcus pyogenes (Lécrivain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion and cited from Lécrivain et al., 2018.

claim: NusG-dependent pausing is a critical component of NusG-dependent termination.
source: Our in vitro results establish that NusG-dependent pausing is a critical component of NusG-dependent termination.
evidence: This is a major conclusion stated in the discussion based on in vitro pausing and termination experiments.

claim: The NusG-dependent pause likely extends the time frame for terminator hairpin completion before readthrough occurs.
source: The NusG-dependent pause likely extends the time frame for terminator hairpin completion before readthrough occurs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: The NusG-dependent pause occurs when RNAP incorporates U residues into the nascent transcript at positions −12, −11, −8, −7, and −6 relative to the 3' end at position −1.
source: This pause is sequence-specific and occurs when RNAP incorporates U residues into the nascent transcript at positions −12, −11, −8, −7, and −6 relative to the 3' end at position −1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The U residues at positions −12 and −11 would always be present in the base of the terminator hairpin.
source: Note that the U residues at positions −12 and −11 would always be present in the base of the terminator hairpin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a structural constraint.

claim: Terminator hairpins with weak terminal base pairs are highly atypical due to the various structural elements of RNAP that stabilize the elongation complex.
source: Terminator hairpins with weak terminal base pairs are highly atypical due to the various structural elements of RNAP that stabilize the elongation complex, including the interactions between the Sw3 pocket and the lid of RNAP with the −10 and −9 positions of the RNA transcript, respectively (Ray-Soni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited from Ray-Soni et al., 2016.

claim: Certain bacterial species evolved a strong G-C preference at the base of the terminator hairpin to drive completion of its formation.
source: Displacement of these interactions requires major energetic expenditures, which may explain why certain bacterial species evolved a strong G-C preference at the base of the terminator hairpin to drive completion of its formation (Ray-Soni et al., 2016; Peters et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Ray-Soni et al., 2016; Peters et al., 2011.

claim: Terminators that depend on the formation of terminal A-U/G-U base pairs require NusG, while terminators that have G-C or C-G terminal base pairs may not be able to induce a sufficiently stable NusG-dependent pause, and therefore will depend solely on NusA.
source: The observation that NusA stimulates termination at a more upstream position provides evidence for a model in which terminators that depend on the formation of terminal A-U/G-U base pairs require NusG, while terminators that have G-C or C-G terminal base pairs may not be able to induce a sufficiently stable NusG-dependent pause, and therefore will depend solely on NusA (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The main feature that differentiates terminators that require NusA and NusG (Req A and G) from terminators that require either NusA or NusG (Req A or G) is hairpin strength, with Req A and G terminators having significantly weaker hairpins than Req A or G terminators.
source: Moreover, our data suggests that the main feature that differentiates terminators that require NusA and NusG (Req A and G) from terminators that require either NusA or NusG (Req A or G) is hairpin strength, with Req A and G terminators having significantly weaker hairpins than Req A or G terminators (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: The most suboptimal terminators (Req A and G) require both the NusG-dependent pause and the hairpin stimulation activity of NusA, while the comparatively more optimal (Req A or G) terminators can function efficiently with only one of these activities.
source: This model suggests that the most suboptimal terminators (Req A and G) require both the NusG-dependent pause and the hairpin stimulation activity of NusA, while the comparatively more optimal (Req A or G) terminators can function efficiently with only one of these activities.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed in the discussion.

claim: A decrease in the expression of the 3' portion of the fla/che operon compared to the 5' portion was previously reported in B. subtilis.
source: A decrease in the expression of the 3' portion of the fla/che operon compared to the 5' portion was previously reported in B. subtilis (Cozy and Kearns, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Cozy and Kearns, 2010.

claim: NusG may function as a processivity factor in B. subtilis.
source: The possibility that NusG functions as a processivity factor in B. subtilis may explain this defect in transcript completion.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: NusA may serve as an anti-processivity factor.
source: Moreover, the fact that NusA depletion alone resulted in an increase in expression across the entire fla/che operon is suggestive that NusA may serve as an anti-processivity factor (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion based on data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Modulating the activity of NusG and/or NusA governs the frequency of completion of the fla/che operon transcript and serves as a method for B. subtilis to regulate the switch between motile and sessile states.
source: These results hint that modulating the activity of NusG and/or NusA governs the frequency of completion of the fla/che operon transcript and serves as a method for B. subtilis to regulate the switch between motile and sessile states.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion.

claim: The ability of NusG to contact the ntDNA strand may be present in a large number of Gram-positive and Gram-negative phyla.
source: A phylogenetic analysis focusing on bacterial species that contain a B. subtilis-like NusG homolog with an NT or HT dipeptide shows that the ability of NusG to contact the ntDNA strand may be present in a large number of Gram-positive and Gram-negative phyla (Figure 9; Yakhnin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mycobacterial NusG contains an NT dipeptide at the position corresponding to the B. subtilis NusG ntDNA contact region.
source: Moreover, mycobacterial NusG was found to contain an NT dipeptide at this position and thus the discovery that mycobacterial NusG stimulates intrinsic termination at suboptimal terminators in vitro (Czyz et al., 2014) suggests that the NusG-dependent termination mechanism may be conserved as well.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and cited from Czyz et al., 2014.

claim: The NusG-dependent termination mechanism may be conserved across bacterial species.
source: Moreover, mycobacterial NusG was found to contain an NT dipeptide at this position and thus the discovery that mycobacterial NusG stimulates intrinsic termination at suboptimal terminators in vitro (Czyz et al., 2014) suggests that the NusG-dependent termination mechanism may be conserved as well.
evidence: This is a speculation stated in the discussion based on phylogenetic analysis and cited work.
